newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-LEONARD'S CHARM IS AS BRIGHT AS EVER.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-LEONARD'S CHARM IS AS BRIGHT AS EVER.

text.p: Next to the word charm in the dictionary there should be a picture of Sugar Ray Leonard.

Of course, the dazzling, toothy smile of the still impish-looking former, five-time world boxing champion wouldn't be all that far from the definition of cloying or even calculating. But then again one person's surfeit of sugar could be someone else's confection of perfection.
As depressing as it may be for those who remember the bubbly fighter winning his gold medal in the 1976 Montreal Olympics, Leonard is 40 now and a grandfather.
And -- in a louder wakeup call for anyone who doesn't think 40 is middle aged -- Sugar Ray Leonard has his prostate checked every year.
Leonard is back -- all 1,000 watts of him -- and he has carefully chosen Hector "Macho" Camacho as his first ring opponent in six years.
The two will fight for something called the International Boxing Council middleweight title. Leonard will receive about $3 million and Camacho $2 million for the scheduled 12-round bout.

The hyperactive 34-year-old Camacho (63-2-1) brings two important things to the fight from Leonard's perspective: a certain draw at the box office as a showcase of tacky self-promotion, and a punch that Pee Wee Herman could walk through.

Leonard, in addition to the fascination many fans may have about how well his once prodigious talents have weathered the years, of course, brings all that charm to sell tickets in the Atlantic City Convention Centre and in living rooms on pay-per-view television.
It's a charm that sometimes is so overwhelming, it seems too good to be true.

He stares in bright-eyed attention at a questioner, thoughtfully frowns as he searches for the right words in response, and then delivers them with a smile that swears on a stack of Wheaties to their sincerity.
After a light workout earlier this week, Leonard was asked why he is fighting again.
"Everyone tells me when you're 40 you should be lying in a rocking chair on the golf course, checking your bladder, if you will," he said with his best Hollywood smile.
"I feel great because I think age is a matter of attitude."
He was an impressive figure with bulging biceps, quick feet and fast hands -- at least against the air.

Overall, however, he appeared a bit smaller in his halcyon years when, as one of the finest welterweights ever, he fought all the big names, such as Wilfredo Benitez, Roberto Duran (three times), Thomas Hearns (twice), and Marvin Hagler.
"When you feel good, when you feel your body become rejuvenated, your mind becomes rejuvenated also," he said referring to the training he began in early December.

"And for me personally, I've been on the assumption that if you're sharp mentally and physically you can do whatever you want to do," said Leonard (36-2-1), whose last fight in 1991 was a loss on a 12-round decision to Terry Norris for the World Boxing Council super welterweight title.
Immediately after that defeat, Leonard grabbed the microphone and announced his third retirement, hastily, he says now.

After looking at the tape of that fight for the first time about eight months ago, Leonard insists Norris did not beat him badly. And Leonard said the emotional instability of a traumatic divorce from his first wife and injured ribs contributed to his loss to Norris.
"My fights are based on my mental stability."

People say, "I've made so much money. Here I have a wonderful family, a dog. I have a white picket fence, a cat. Why would I do that" because they feel all those wonderful things that I have is a prerequisite for happiness.
"Happiness for me is doing what I want to do when I want to do it. And even though there's concern because of the risk, because of the nature of my sport. That's what has made me who I am today.
"It's as simple as going back to my old job. I don't want to ask myself a couple of years from now what would have happened if..." Leonard said. Now at "the tender age of 40, it's like now or never."

Leonard admits to the dangers of his old job, which resulted in a detached retina, since repaired. But it's a risk he readily assumes and hopes to minimise by taking extremely good care of his health with frequent medical tests. "Once a year I have my prostate checked," he said with a little laugh.
Leonard said he doesn't have a particular plan to fight Camacho. But sooner or later "we will exchange and he'll test my strength."
It's a good thing for Camacho that he doesn't have to test all that charm.
